rationale.conceptual: The underlying method is an established multiscale approach (NEMD + FE) with published protocols. The conceptual challenge lies in correctly setting up non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (thermostat, temperature gradient, extrapolation) and translating the experimental grain-boundary configurations into precise atomistic and continuum models. No new equations are derived; the difficulty is in the precise assembly of known components.
rationale.execution: The pipeline requires: generating multiple atomistic models (various lengths, three interface types), running LAMMPS NEMD simulations with the REBO potential for each configuration, post-processing temperature profiles and energy fluxes, performing linear extrapolation, building finite element meshes with random triangular tessellation and interface conductance contacts, and solving steady-state heat conduction across a parameter sweep. This involves 7+ distinct stages, multiple tools (LAMMPS, Python, FEniCS/Abaqus) and careful data handoffs.

difficulty.reasoning: The paper combines standard NEMD (non-equilibrium molecular dynamics) with finite element modeling to compute thermal conductivity of MoS₂ heterostructures. The method is not novel in concept but requires careful implementation of molecular dynamics parameters (REBO potential, thermostatting, extrapolation) and multi-stage finite element model construction. Execution involves multiple simulation steps (model generation, MD runs for several lengths and interfaces, post-processing, FE meshing, and solving), making it a moderately complex multi-tool pipeline.

compute_estimate.reasoning: Classical MD simulations with the REBO potential are CPU-bound and operate on systems of a few thousand atoms; memory footprint is low (a few GB). The finite element models are 2D with ~1000 triangles, requiring negligible memory. No large datasets or GPU acceleration is required.
